title: United Kingdom
answer: The United Kingdom brings four parts together: England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland. The first three share the island called Great Britain. Northern Ireland is across the Irish Sea on a different island, which it shares with the Republic of Ireland. London, on the River Thames, is the United Kingdom’s capital. Traveling north or west from some of the flatter parts of England brings you into much hillier country.
facts: The United Kingdom’s only land border is between Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland.

title: Ireland
answer: Ireland can mean an island in the Atlantic or the country that covers most of it. The country’s capital, Dublin, is on the east coast. A broad plain fills much of the middle of the island, with hills and mountains scattered around the edges. The River Shannon drains much of the middle and flows to the Atlantic. The island’s damp, mild weather helps grasses grow, which is one reason green fields are such a familiar sight there.
facts: Irish and English are official languages of the country.

title: Portugal
answer: Portugal looks mostly west toward the Atlantic Ocean. On land it borders Spain, and together the two countries cover most of the Iberian Peninsula. Lisbon, Portugal’s capital, sits where the Tagus River spreads out before reaching the sea. The Portuguese islands of Madeira and the Azores are farther out in the Atlantic. Many travelers first picture the sunny coast, but northern Portugal also has hills and cooler, wetter country.

facts: Both the Azores and Madeira are groups of islands separated from mainland Portugal by ocean.

title: Spain
answer: Find the part of Europe that sticks down between the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea. Spain fills most of it, and Madrid, the capital, sits well inland. The central part of the country is high and broad, so living in inland Spain can feel very different from living beside the sea. The Pyrenees rise near France. Spain also includes the Canary Islands in the Atlantic and the Balearic Islands in the Mediterranean.
facts: Portugal and Spain share the Iberian Peninsula.

title: Germany
answer: Germany stretches from low country on the North Sea and Baltic Sea to mountains near the Alps. Its capital, Berlin, is in the northeast. In western Germany the Rhine passes settlements, farmland, and busy ports. Rivers like the Rhine let boats carry large loads far inland, even when a town is nowhere near the ocean. Germany shares land borders with nine countries, so a trip in many different directions can take you to a neighboring nation.
facts: The Danube begins in Germany and runs east across Europe.

title: Netherlands
answer: The Netherlands lies on the North Sea, where several European rivers reach the coast. Much of the ground is low and flat. Long banks keep water away from some towns and fields, and pumps move extra water out of land that would otherwise stay too wet. Amsterdam is the capital, while the national government meets in The Hague. In maps and conversations you may hear Holland, which is a name for two provinces within the Netherlands.
aliases: what is the difference between Holland and the Netherlands
facts: The Rhine, Meuse, and Scheldt reach the North Sea in the region around the Netherlands.

title: Belgium
answer: Belgium sits between France, the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg, and the North Sea. Flat land near the coast gives way to higher, wooded country in the southeast. Brussels is the capital and a meeting place for European Union leaders and officials. Dutch, French, and German are official languages. Which one you hear most depends on where you are: much of northern Belgium uses Dutch, while French is widespread in the south.
facts: The upland region in southeastern Belgium is called the Ardennes.

title: Luxembourg
answer: Luxembourg fits between Belgium, France, and Germany. The country and its capital city share the name Luxembourg. In the north you can find part of the Ardennes, an upland area with wooded hills and river valleys. The Moselle River makes up part of the border with Germany to the east. A student in Luxembourg may hear and use more than one language during a school day, and multilingual signs are common.
facts: Luxembourg has no seacoast.

questions.text: Which larger neighbor also includes the Ardennes?

title: Switzerland
answer: Switzerland sits among mountains and lakes in central Europe. The Alps cover much of the south, and many towns sit on the flatter land farther north and west. Bern is the federal city, the place where the national government meets. The Rhine starts in the Swiss Alps and eventually reaches the North Sea. A river that reaches the sea can start far from it: Switzerland itself has no coast.
facts: Switzerland recognizes German, French, Italian, and Romansh as national languages.

title: Austria
answer: If you cross Austria from west to east, the tall ridges of the Alps give way to lower land around Vienna, the capital. The Danube flows through Vienna and continues toward the Black Sea, passing through or beside several countries. Mountains affect how people travel. A route along a river valley can make for a gentler journey than climbing across every ridge. Austria has many mountains and no coast of its own.
facts: Vienna sits in the eastern part of Austria.

Where does the Danube begin its long trip?

title: Italy
answer: Italy reaches into the Mediterranean on a peninsula often compared with a boot. The Alps curve across the north, and the Apennine Mountains follow much of the length of the peninsula. Rome, Italy’s capital, is near the middle of the western side. Sicily and Sardinia are large Italian islands. The shape of the country gives it long stretches of coast, while the mountains make travel between some nearby places harder than a flat map suggests.
facts: Mount Etna is an active volcano on Sicily.

title: Malta
answer: Malta is a small country made up of islands in the Mediterranean Sea, south of Sicily. The two largest islands are Malta and Gozo. Valletta, the capital, sits on a narrow ridge between two harbors. On a map it is easy to see why ships could find shelter beside the city. Malta’s rocky ground and limited fresh water also make the sea important in a very different way from how it is for a country with many rivers.
facts: Maltese and English are official languages.

questions.text: Which country includes Sicily, the island north of Malta?

What changes the water level at a harbor?

title: Greece
answer: Greece lies at the southern end of the Balkan Peninsula, and its land reaches far into the sea through islands and smaller peninsulas. Athens, the capital, is on the mainland near the coast. Crete lies much farther south than Athens. Greece’s islands are separated by water, and steep hills and mountains break up much of the mainland, so boats and roads both matter when people travel from place to place.
facts: Mount Olympus is the highest mountain in Greece.

title: Denmark
answer: Denmark connects with mainland Europe through the Jutland Peninsula, which borders Germany. Much of the rest of the country is on islands. Copenhagen, the capital, lies mostly on the island of Zealand, near Sweden across a narrow stretch of water. This is a country where bridges and ferries can bring together towns that are close on a map but separated by the sea. Much of Denmark’s land is low and gently rolling.
facts: Mainland Denmark has one land neighbor, Germany.

questions.text: Which country is across the water from Copenhagen?

Which nearby country has much higher mountains and deep inlets?

title: Norway
answer: Norway is a long, narrow country on the west side of the Scandinavian Peninsula. In many places the sea reaches inland between high rocky slopes. These long inlets are called fjords. Ice once moved through the valleys and carved them deeper, and seawater later filled them. Oslo, the capital, is in the south. Far in the north, some places get weeks in summer when the Sun never sets.
facts: Norway lies west of Sweden, and it also borders Finland and Russia.

title: Sweden
answer: Sweden fills much of the eastern side of the Scandinavian Peninsula. It borders Norway, and some of Sweden’s highest land is close to that border. Rivers and lakes break up the land farther east, and islands are scattered along parts of the coast. Stockholm, the capital, stands partly on islands where Lake Mälaren meets the sea. Waterways help explain why a boat can sometimes be as useful as a road there.
facts: Gotland is a Swedish island in the Baltic Sea.

questions.text: Which country takes up the western side of the Scandinavian Peninsula?

title: Finland
answer: Finland has thousands of lakes, many among forests in the southern and central parts of the country. In the last ice age, moving ice scoured the ground. After the ice retreated, water filled many of the low spots. Helsinki, the capital, is on the southern coast, while Finland stretches far north beyond the Arctic Circle. A long drive north can take you from a busy Baltic port to a place where the summer Sun stays up all night.
facts: Finnish and Swedish are Finland’s official national languages.

questions.text: Which country lies on the other side of some of Finland’s western waters?

title: Iceland
answer: Iceland is an island in the North Atlantic where very old ice and new volcanic rock can be found in the same country. Glaciers cover stretches of the interior, while heat close to the surface warms water underground. Reykjavík, the capital, lies near the southwest coast. Iceland sits on a long ridge in the Atlantic where two pieces of Earth’s outer shell pull apart, and the movement helps make it volcanically active.
facts: Vatnajökull is a large ice cap in southeastern Iceland.

title: Poland
answer: Much of Poland is broad and low, with the Baltic Sea to the north and mountain ranges rising near its southern borders. Warsaw, the capital, stands beside the Vistula River. The river starts in the south and eventually runs to the Baltic. Following it on a map shows how a river can link mountains, farming areas, and a capital city before opening out near the sea.
facts: Poland and Slovakia share some of the high Tatra Mountains.

title: Czechia
answer: Czechia, also called the Czech Republic, sits in central Europe and has no coast. It contains the historic regions of Bohemia and Moravia and part of Silesia. Prague, the capital, grew along the Vltava River. The Vltava joins the Elbe, which flows onward through Germany to the sea. People and goods can travel across a country’s borders along a river, even when the country where the journey starts is far from any ocean.
facts: Czechia and Slovakia were once parts of one country, Czechoslovakia.

Which landlocked country is directly south of Czechia?

title: Slovakia
answer: Slovakia lies in central Europe, much of it in the Carpathian Mountains. The Tatras along the Polish border have some especially high peaks. The landscape gets lower toward the Danube in the southwest. Bratislava, the capital, stands on the Danube near Austria and Hungary. A traveler standing in Bratislava can be close to several countries at once, even though Slovakia has no coast.
facts: Slovakia and Czechia became separate countries in 1993.

title: Hungary
answer: Most of Hungary is in a low basin surrounded by higher land in central Europe. The Danube divides Budapest, the capital, into parts that grew separately and are now connected by bridges. On a map of western Hungary, long Lake Balaton is easy to pick out. Flat land across much of the country has room for large fields, while hills and smaller mountains rise in some other parts.
facts: Hungary has no ocean coast, but the Danube connects it with other countries.

title: Slovenia
answer: Slovenia sits where parts of the Alps, the plains of central Europe, and the coast of the Adriatic come close together. Ljubljana, the capital, is inland. In some parts of Slovenia, rainwater slowly dissolves certain rocks and leaves caves and openings underneath. In hills like these, a stream can even disappear below the ground and flow through a cave before coming back to the surface.
facts: Slovenia has a short coast on the Adriatic Sea between Italy and Croatia.

title: Croatia
answer: Croatia curves around part of the Adriatic Sea. On the coast, many islands lie just offshore and some long ones run roughly the same direction as the shore. The capital, Zagreb, is inland in the north, among a different landscape of hills, valleys, and flatter country. Croatia’s shape leaves some places near the sea quite far from Zagreb, so looking at a map helps explain why the country feels different from one end to the other.
facts: Italy is across the Adriatic from Croatia.

title: Romania
answer: Romania stretches from the curve of the Carpathian Mountains to the Black Sea. Its capital, Bucharest, lies on lower land south of the mountains. Near the sea the Danube spreads into channels around wet islands and reeds. This low, watery area is a delta. Water and mud that started far upriver can reach the delta, and the channels carry the river out into the Black Sea.
facts: Romania and Bulgaria share a long stretch of border along the Danube.

title: Bulgaria
answer: Bulgaria lies in southeastern Europe, with the Black Sea on the east side and part of the Danube along the north. The Balkan Mountains cross the middle of the country from west to east. Sofia, the capital, lies in the west, in a broad valley with mountains nearby. Travel south and you reach Greece or Türkiye, while traveling north in many parts of Bulgaria takes you to the Danube and across it to Romania.

title: Estonia
answer: Estonia is the northernmost of the three countries often grouped as the Baltic states. Tallinn, the capital, stands on the Gulf of Finland. Helsinki is across the water to the north. Much of Estonia is low, with forests, wet bogs, and a coast broken into islands. On the eastern side Lake Peipus is shared with Russia. A traveler can cross the country from a sea port to a large freshwater lake.

title: Latvia
answer: Latvia sits between Estonia and Lithuania on the eastern side of the Baltic Sea. Riga, the capital, stands near the mouth of the Daugava River on the Gulf of Riga. The river begins far to the east, crosses Latvia, and then becomes part of a wide stretch of water open to the Baltic. Much of Latvia is low country, with forests and rivers and a coast along both the gulf and the open sea.
facts: The western shore of Latvia faces the open Baltic Sea.

title: Lithuania
answer: Lithuania is the southernmost of the three Baltic states. Vilnius, the capital, is inland near the southeastern part of the country. Near the coast, the Curonian Spit forms a skinny strip of sand with the Baltic Sea on one side and a shallow lagoon on the other. Wind moves dry sand on those narrow shores into dunes. Farther inland, the country has lakes, forests, and gently rolling farmland.

title: Argentina
answer: Argentina runs down the eastern side of the Andes for much of southern South America. Near Buenos Aires, the capital, the land opens into grassy plains called the Pampas. Farther south is Patagonia, with wide, windy spaces and mountains and ice nearer the Andes. Argentina’s long shape helps explain the big differences between the warmer forests in the north and the cold landscapes near the continent’s southern tip.
facts: Aconcagua, in Argentina, is the highest peak in the Andes.

title: Chile
answer: Chile is a remarkably long and narrow country between the Andes and the Pacific Ocean. Its northern Atacama Desert is so dry that some places rarely see rain. Near Santiago, the capital, cooler wet winters and drier summers help shape a very different landscape. Farther south, glaciers and narrow arms of the sea break up the coast. A map of Chile can look like a ribbon beside a high wall.

title: Uruguay
answer: Uruguay lies between Brazil and Argentina, on the side of South America that faces the Atlantic Ocean. Much of it is made up of gently rolling plains and low hills. The capital, Montevideo, overlooks the broad Río de la Plata. Fresh water from inland rivers mixes with salty ocean water in this wide opening. Inland, cattle and sheep can graze across a landscape that is far flatter than the Andes.
facts: The Uruguay River forms much of the country’s border with Argentina.

title: Paraguay
answer: The Paraguay River runs down through the country that shares its name. To the west lies part of the Gran Chaco, a broad landscape where many places are dry and hot. To the east, rolling country gets more rain and holds many of the country’s farms and towns. Asunción, the capital, stands beside the river. Paraguay has no sea coast, but rivers connect it to countries farther downstream.
facts: Paraguay borders Argentina, Bolivia, and Brazil.

title: Bolivia
answer: Bolivia’s landscapes include high mountains, a wide plateau called the Altiplano, and low land toward the Amazon basin. In the west, the country shares Lake Titicaca with Peru. Two cities have capital roles: Sucre is the constitutional capital, and La Paz is where the national government’s executive and legislature work. A trip from the lowlands up into the Andes can make the air and temperature feel suddenly different.

title: Peru
answer: Peru runs along the Pacific coast of South America. Lima, the capital, is along the dry coastal strip. Farther inland, the Andes rise sharply, and on the eastern side of those high mountains, water flows toward the Amazon. That is why Peru can contain dry coast, cold mountain slopes, and tropical forest at the same time. Looking only at the coastline would leave out two very different parts of Peru.

title: Ecuador
answer: Ecuador takes its name from the equator, the imaginary line that crosses the country. Quito, the capital, sits high in the Andes, where the elevation keeps conditions cooler than people might expect near that line. Ecuador also includes warm lowlands, part of the Amazon basin, and the Galápagos Islands in the Pacific. To visit all these landscapes, you would travel a long way east and west as well as up and down.

title: Colombia
answer: Colombia is in the northwest corner of South America. It is the continent’s only country with coasts on both the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea. Its capital, Bogotá, sits high in the Andes, and the mountains divide into several chains as they approach the coast. Rivers between the mountains reach into the lowlands, where the climate and landscape can be quite different from those around the capital.
facts: Colombia shares a land border with Panama, where Central America meets South America.

title: Venezuela
answer: Venezuela has a Caribbean coast, a big river basin inland, and striking flat-topped mountains in the southeast. In parts of the interior, the Orinoco River flows past wide grassy plains called the Llanos. Farther south and east, some cliffs drop far enough that a waterfall can break into mist before the water reaches the bottom. The capital, Caracas, sits among mountains near the Caribbean coast.
facts: The water of the Orinoco River reaches the Atlantic through a delta.

title: Guyana
answer: Guyana lies on the Atlantic side of northern South America, east of Venezuela and west of Suriname. Much of its population lives on the narrow coastal plain, where Georgetown, the capital, stands near the mouth of the Demerara River. Inland, rivers cross forests and rise toward highland country. Guyana is part of South America, and it has strong links with Caribbean countries, including sharing English as an official language with many of them.

title: Suriname
answer: Suriname faces the Atlantic Ocean on the north side of South America. The capital, Paramaribo, is near the coast on the Suriname River. Much of the land farther inland is forested, and rivers are an important way of reaching places there. Dutch is the official language, and people also speak several other languages. On a world map, Suriname and the Netherlands look far apart, while the languages show a historical connection.

facts: Suriname borders Guyana, Brazil, and French Guiana.

title: Panama
answer: Panama is a narrow country between the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean. Its shape makes it part of the land bridge connecting Central and South America. People built the Panama Canal across that land so ships could pass between the two bodies of water without sailing around the whole continent. Panama City, the country’s capital, is near the Pacific end. The country has hills and forest as well as the famous shipping route.
aliases: country connecting Central and South America
facts: Panama has land borders with Costa Rica and Colombia.

title: Costa Rica
answer: Costa Rica runs between the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea in Central America. Mountains and volcanoes rise through the middle, and San José, the capital, is in the central part of the country. A trip from one side to the other can pass beaches, wet forests, and much cooler heights. Changes in height and rain help make room for many different kinds of plants and animals within a small area.

facts: Costa Rica borders Nicaragua to the north and Panama to the southeast.

title: Nicaragua
answer: Nicaragua’s west side has volcanoes and two large lakes close to the Pacific coast. Managua, the capital, is beside the smaller Lake Managua. Lake Nicaragua lies farther southeast and is much larger. On the other side of the country, rivers head through flatter land toward the Caribbean. A single country can therefore have separate groups of rivers whose water eventually reaches opposite sides of Central America.

title: Honduras
answer: Honduras has a long coast on the Caribbean Sea and a much shorter coast beside the Gulf of Fonseca, which opens to the Pacific. Mountains take up much of the land between the two sides. Tegucigalpa, the capital, is in the hilly south-central area. The Bay Islands lie off the northern shore, separated from the mainland by Caribbean waters, so part of a trip there has to cross the sea.
facts: Honduras has a land border with Guatemala, El Salvador, and Nicaragua.

title: El Salvador
answer: El Salvador lies on the Pacific side of Central America. Unlike many of its neighbors, it has no Caribbean coast. San Salvador, the capital, stands inland near a volcano. Mountains and valleys cover much of the country, and a lower strip of land runs beside the ocean. In a small area like this, a traveler can go from flat, warm coast to high volcanic slopes without traveling hundreds of miles.
aliases: which Central American country has no Caribbean coast

title: Guatemala
answer: Guatemala reaches south from Mexico into Central America. It has low forested country in the north and a chain of mountains and volcanoes closer to the Pacific. Guatemala City, the capital, lies inland in the highlands. The country also reaches a small piece of Caribbean coast in the east. Changes in height give the country both warm lowlands and cooler areas where many of its towns and cities grew.
facts: The country’s high peaks include the volcano Tajumulco.

title: Belize
answer: Belize faces the Caribbean Sea on the eastern side of Central America. A long coral reef lies offshore, with small islands, shallow water, and much deeper sea not far apart. On land, there are low plains near the shore and the Maya Mountains farther inland. Belmopan, the capital, is inland. It has a different setting from Belize City, the larger former capital, which is right on the coast.
facts: English is the official language of Belize.

title: Cuba
answer: Cuba is an island country at the northern edge of the Caribbean. The largest island stretches far from west to east, and many smaller islands and reefs lie nearby. Havana, the capital, faces north across the water toward Florida. Much of Cuba is relatively low, but mountains rise in the southeast. Because the island sits between several large bodies of water, its coast has been important to people sailing between them.
facts: The highest part of Cuba is in the Sierra Maestra mountains.

title: Jamaica
answer: Jamaica is an island in the Caribbean Sea south of Cuba. Its capital, Kingston, is on the southeast coast beside a large natural harbor. Behind it the Blue Mountains rise sharply, and other parts of the island have hills of limestone, caves, and streams. The shift from sunny coast to higher and cooler ground helps explain why the island can have more than one kind of landscape within a short distance.
facts: Blue Mountain Peak is the highest point in Jamaica.

title: Haiti
answer: Haiti covers the western part of Hispaniola, an island it shares with the Dominican Republic. Its capital, Port-au-Prince, sits beside a sheltered bay on the western side. Much of the country is mountainous, with valleys and plains between the ranges. Hispaniola also lies near the edges of large moving pieces of Earth’s outer shell. When those pieces suddenly slip past each other, they can shake the ground across both countries.
facts: Haitian Creole and French are official languages in Haiti.

title: Dominican Republic
answer: The Dominican Republic covers the eastern part of Hispaniola, sharing that island with Haiti. Its capital, Santo Domingo, is on the Caribbean coast, on the south side of the island. Mountain ranges rise inland and leave room for valleys and farmland between them. A country bordered by warm sea can still have chilly places high in the mountains, where the air and ground are much farther above sea level.

title: The Bahamas
answer: The Bahamas are a chain of islands and low sandy islets in the Atlantic near Florida and Cuba. Many sit on underwater banks where the sea is shallow and can look pale blue from above. Nassau, the capital, is on the island of New Providence. Only some of the islands are settled. With broad stretches of shallow water between them, boats have long mattered for moving people and supplies.

title: Trinidad and Tobago
answer: Trinidad and Tobago are two main islands at the southern end of the Caribbean. Trinidad, the larger island, lies just off Venezuela, across a narrow stretch of water. Port of Spain, the capital, is on Trinidad beside the Gulf of Paria. Tobago lies northeast of Trinidad. title: China
answer: China covers a large part of eastern Asia. Its land generally steps down from high plateaus and mountains in the west to broad lowlands and a long coast in the east. The Yangtze flows from high country to the sea near Shanghai, carrying water across much of China. Beijing, the capital, is farther north. China’s large size makes room for many landscapes, from some of the world’s highest mountains to warm coastal country.

title: Mongolia
answer: Mongolia sits in inland Asia between Russia and China. The Gobi Desert takes up part of the south, while wide grasslands spread across much of the country. Mountains rise in the west and north. Ulaanbaatar, the capital, stands in a valley in the north-central part of Mongolia, where winters can be very cold. Pyongyang, the capital, lies on the Taedong River in the west. The peninsula touches the sea on both sides, but toward the north the country has land borders with China and Russia. Seoul, the capital, is in the northwest and grew around the Han River. The long coastline includes many islands, especially toward the south and west. title: Nepal
answer: Nepal follows the southern slopes of the Himalayas between India and China. Along its southern side the ground is much lower and flatter. answer: Bhutan lies in the eastern Himalayas between India and China. Along the south, lower hills rise above the plains of India. Farther north, high ridges and peaks can stay covered with snow. Thimphu, the capital, is in a river valley in western Bhutan. Roads that look short on a map may have to bend around ridges, so a trip across Bhutan can take longer than the distance suggests.

title: Bangladesh
answer: Much of Bangladesh sits on the low land where several large Asian rivers meet and flow into the Bay of Bengal. Water and silt from far away in the Himalayas can reach the fields and channels of this delta. Dhaka, the capital, is in the central part of the country. answer: Pakistan stretches from some of the world’s highest mountains in the north to the Arabian Sea in the south. The Indus River runs down through the country and brings water to many fields. Much of the land near the river is drier than the fields might look, so farmers use channels and other ways to get water to their crops. Islamabad, the capital, sits farther north near the foothills.

title: Sri Lanka
answer: Sri Lanka is a large island just south of India in the Indian Ocean. Low coastal areas surround higher country in the middle of the island. Tea is grown in some of the cooler hills, while rainfall and temperature vary from place to place. Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte houses the country’s parliament near Colombo, a large port city. title: Thailand
answer: Thailand stands in mainland Southeast Asia and extends south down part of the Malay Peninsula. Its capital, Bangkok, grew beside the Chao Phraya River, whose low plain contains fields and many settlements. The north is higher and hillier, and the southern peninsula has coasts on both sides. title: Vietnam

Hanoi, the capital, lies near the Red River in the north. In the south, many channels of the Mekong spread across flat ground before meeting the sea. answer: Laos is the only country in mainland Southeast Asia without a coast. Much of it is mountainous, but many settlements lie close to river valleys. Vientiane, the capital, stands beside the Mekong River, which forms a long part of the border with Thailand. The river continues through Cambodia and Vietnam to the sea. title: Myanmar

The Ayeyarwady River flows south through much of the country, passing wide farming areas and spreading into a delta near the coast. answer: Senegal lies on the Atlantic at the far western side of Africa. Dakar, the capital, stands on a peninsula poking into the ocean. The Senegal River follows part of the northern boundary. Farther south, a different river is surrounded by The Gambia, a long narrow country with its own small coast. A map of both countries helps show how water can shape the outline of land boundaries as well as coastlines.
facts: Senegal surrounds The Gambia on three sides.

title: The Gambia
answer: The Gambia is a long, narrow country in western Africa, with the Gambia River running through most of it. Senegal surrounds the land borders, and at its western end the river reaches the Atlantic Ocean. Banjul, the capital, lies near the river mouth. In many places it is easier to picture the country by following the river on a map than by trying to recognize its outline alone.
facts: The Gambia’s long shape follows the course of a river rather than a mountain range.

title: Ghana
answer: Ghana faces the Gulf of Guinea in western Africa. Accra, the capital, lies beside the sea, and the land stretches inland to drier plains in the north. Lake Volta takes up a broad part of the east. It formed when a dam held back water in the Volta River system. The country’s coast has ports, while hundreds of miles of rivers and roads connect settlements inland.

title: New Zealand
answer: New Zealand lies in the southwestern Pacific Ocean and includes two main islands. A narrow passage called Cook Strait separates them. Wellington, the capital, is at the southern end of the North Island. The Southern Alps rise on the South Island, and there are active volcanoes in the North Island. Mountain weather can change quickly over a short distance, even though the surrounding ocean helps give many coastal places generally mild temperatures.
facts: Aoraki or Mount Cook is New Zealand’s highest peak.

title: Fiji
answer: Fiji is a group of islands in the South Pacific. The two largest, Viti Levu and Vanua Levu, have hills and valleys, while many smaller islands sit close to coral reefs. Suva, the capital, is on Viti Levu. A traveler can cross rugged land by road and then have to take a boat for what looks like a short distance on the map, because the country’s settlements are spread across separate islands.
facts: Fiji’s islands are mostly south of the equator.

title: Samoa
answer: Samoa is an island country in the central South Pacific. Its two largest islands, Upolu and Savaiʻi, rose from volcanic activity. Forested hills stand inland, and many settlements are by the shore. Apia, the capital, is on Upolu. Farther east are the islands of American Samoa, a different political area. The similar names describe neighbors, and looking for Apia or Pago Pago on a map helps tell them apart.
facts: Savaiʻi is the larger of Samoa’s two main islands by area.

title: Tonga
answer: Tonga is an island kingdom that stretches north and south through part of the South Pacific. Some islands are low and made mostly of rock built up by coral. Others are volcanic and have much higher land. Nukuʻalofa, the capital, is on Tongatapu, the main island in the southern group. The country’s shape is easy to miss on a globe: its many islands occupy only small spots in a much larger stretch of ocean.

title: Altitude
answer: Altitude describes how high something is compared with a chosen level. Maps often measure land height from sea level. Planes can also report how high they are above the ground directly below them, which is a different number. Higher in the air, there is less air pressing down, so the air is thinner. A breath at the top of a tall mountain contains less oxygen than a breath of the same size beside the sea.

facts: Two airplanes at the same height above sea level can be different heights above the ground below them.

title: Andes Mountains
answer: The Andes run like a high spine along the western side of South America. Far below the coast, a large piece of the ocean floor slides beneath the edge of the continent. That movement helps lift and squeeze rock, and it also helps feed eruptions in parts of the range. Hills, wide valleys, icy peaks, and even parts of great deserts belong to this long chain, so crossing it can take you through several climates.
facts: The Andes are the longest mountain range on land.

title: Himalayas
answer: The Himalayas stretch across southern Asia and contain many of Earth’s highest mountains. They started growing when the land carrying India pushed into the land to the north. The two pieces of land were so thick that rock bent, broke, and piled up instead of simply vanishing below the surface. The land is still moving, so the range is still changing. Streams from its slopes join rivers that flow into several countries.
facts: Mount Everest is the tallest peak in the Himalayas.

title: Sahara Desert
answer: The Sahara is a huge dry region that stretches across northern Africa from the Atlantic side toward the Red Sea. Its landscape includes flat rocky areas, mountains, patches of dunes, and places where water helps people and plants survive. A patch of dunes can move as wind piles sand on one side and lets it fall on the other. Much of the desert is so dry that plants grow far apart.

facts: The Sahara is the largest hot desert on Earth.

title: Amazon River
answer: The Amazon begins with streams in the Andes and grows as more rivers join it on the way east. Rain falling across a wide part of South America feeds its huge river system. In wetter times of year, water can spread beyond the river’s banks into parts of the forest. Where the Amazon reaches the Atlantic, it sends enough fresh water into the ocean to affect conditions well beyond the river’s mouth.

facts: The Amazon carries more water to the ocean than any other river on Earth.

title: Nile River
answer: The Nile flows north through northeastern Africa to the Mediterranean. The Blue Nile carries water from Ethiopia, and the White Nile brings water from areas farther south. The two meet at Khartoum in Sudan. Downstream, the river crosses some very dry country. Near the sea, branches spread across a delta built in part from mud the river carried. That mud can make good soil for farmers.
facts: The Nile reaches the Mediterranean on Egypt’s coast.

title: Galápagos Islands
answer: The Galápagos Islands lie far west of Ecuador’s mainland in the Pacific. Eruptions built the islands from the seafloor, so they were separated from the continent from the start. Plants and animals arrived over water in different ways, and their descendants changed over many generations. Some became different from living things elsewhere. Charles Darwin’s visit helped him think about how animals on separate islands can develop different shapes and habits.

title: Lake Baikal
answer: Lake Baikal in Siberia is the deepest lake in the world. Looking at the thin shape it makes on a map gives little hint of how much water is below the surface. The deep opening formed as large areas of rock moved apart. Baikal has fresh water and is home to some animals that live nowhere else, including a seal that spends its life far from any ocean.
facts: At its deepest, Lake Baikal is roughly a mile deep.

title: Grand Canyon
answer: The Grand Canyon is a huge cut through rock in northern Arizona. Far below its rim, the Colorado River has been lifting and carrying away pieces of rock for millions of years. Rain and rockslides help widen the sides as the river keeps cutting. The canyon walls show stripes of different rocks. Some rock near the bottom is much older than the canyon itself, because it was already there when the river began cutting down.
facts: Parts of the canyon are over a mile deep.

title: Antarctic Ice Sheet
answer: Most of Antarctica is covered by a layer of ice thick enough to hide mountains and valleys beneath it. It formed as falling snow piled up over a very long time, squashing the air out of older layers and turning them into ice. The ice moves slowly toward the edges under its own weight. This sheet sits on land, while much of the ice around it floats on the ocean.

title: Caribbean Sea
answer: The Caribbean Sea is a warm part of the Atlantic between Central America, northern South America, and a chain of islands. Cuba, Jamaica, and Hispaniola sit near its northern side. Near its eastern edge, smaller islands form a curved line with openings where water moves between the Caribbean and the wider Atlantic. The sea has deep parts, shallow reefs, and busy routes used by ships traveling between its islands and coasts.

title: Victoria Falls
answer: The Zambezi River spreads wide at the border of Zambia and Zimbabwe, then suddenly pours into a deep, narrow crack in the rock. The water hits with enough force to throw fine drops high above the cliffs. Wind blows this mist onto nearby land, watering plants even when rain has not fallen there. The volume of water changes with the season, so the falls do not always look exactly the same.
facts: Mosi-oa-Tunya is one of the local names for the falls, often translated as “the smoke that thunders.”

title: Mount Kilimanjaro
answer: Mount Kilimanjaro rises from the plains of northern Tanzania to the highest point in Africa. It is made of several volcanoes joined together. A climber passes through different environments, from wooded mountain slopes into cold, mostly bare country near the top. That change happens in a surprisingly short distance because the trail climbs so high. Near the equator the lowlands can be warm while the summit is cold enough for ice.
facts: Kilimanjaro’s highest point is nearly 5,900 meters above sea level.

title: Great Barrier Reef
answer: The Great Barrier Reef lies off Australia’s northeastern coast. It is made of thousands of separate reefs rather than one long unbroken wall. Small coral animals build hard skeletons, and over time new generations grow onto the old structures. The reefs leave hiding places and feeding spots for many animals. On a map some parts of the system meet open ocean, while others protect shallower stretches of sea closer to the shore.
